name: metajson (iod::metajson)
workload: Encoding/decoding C++ structs and vectors whose structure is known at compile time, compared to nlohmann/json and RapidJSON
claimed_speedup: Up to 9x faster than nlohmann/json and 2x faster than RapidJSON (author states these numbers are not from a comprehensive benchmark)
tradeoffs: Only handles JSON objects whose structure is known at compile time (no dynamic/schema-less JSON); no explicit error reporting for malformed JSON; also claims up to 8x smaller binaries than nlohmann/json and 2x smaller than RapidJSON
caveats: Author explicitly states the performance numbers are not from a comprehensive benchmark and are only a rough estimate ('does not take into account the fact that other libraries provide more features'); no hardware stated; project has had no commits since 2019
found_via: Hacker News: query "faster than RapidJSON" surfaced "C++17 MetaJSON 0.1, up to 2x faster than rapidjson"

name: jist
workload: Extracting a single key-path value (last array element) from large JSON/NDJSON files (3.3GB and 28.9GB synthetic inputs)
claimed_speedup: 3.3GB file: 2.05s vs jq 34.17s (~16.7x), 1600MB/s vs 96MB/s throughput, 4.5GB vs 18GB memory; 28.9GB file: 1:30 for jist vs jq unable to complete (out of RAM)
compiler_and_flags: Rust benchmark data generator built with 'cargo build --release'; exact compiler/flags used to build jist itself not stated
tradeoffs: Uses simdjson internally (does not itself beat simdjson) and falls back to a much slower (~300MB/s) character-based lexer for files >4.2GB or forced streaming mode; jq has vastly broader query capability than jist's single key-path extraction
caveats: First-party benchmark on the project's own repo, single synthetic workload shape, only compared against jq (not against simdjson/RapidJSON/nlohmann directly), exact compiler version/flags for the jist binary itself not documented
found_via: Hacker News: query "JSON parser faster than simdjson" surfaced "Show HN: Jist now searches JSON 17x faster than jq"

name: Tachyon JSON (Rust, TachyonConcepts)
workload: Encoding a small fixed JSON object ({"message":"Hello, world!"}) over 1,000,000 iterations, zero-copy serde_json vs Tachyon buffer encode
tradeoffs: Requires unsafe code and manual opt-in for escaping (tachyon_object_noescape! skips escaping by default); fixed-size stack buffer (TachyonBuffer<N>); appears to be a serializer only, no documented parser
caveats: No CPU model, compiler version, or build flags stated; single trivial fixed-message microbenchmark; 0 stars, very small/early project; distinct repo from mrcodechef/Tachyon.JSON which is already on the known list
found_via: Hacker News: query "JSON parser C++ SIMD" surfaced a Tachyon.JSON HN story, which led to `gh search repos "Tachyon.JSON"` turning up this separate Rust project

name: fastgron
workload: Converting large JSON files into greppable gron-style discrete key=value assignments ("JSON to GRON") on big files
claimed_speedup: 50x faster than gron on big files (400MB/s input / 1.8GB/s output on an M1 MacBook Pro)
tradeoffs: Built on simdjson internally (does not itself beat simdjson); gron is a Go, single-threaded tool, so this is a JSON-processing-tool comparison rather than a raw parser/library comparison
caveats: Compiler and build flags not stated; the claim is a first-party README statement without a linked reproducible benchmark script visible in the README
found_via: Hacker News: query "fastest JSON library C++" surfaced "Show HN: fastgron: A JSON to GRON Converter That's 40 Times Faster Than Gron"
